title: Capt. James Estill / Estill's Defeat
summary: On March 22, 1782, Capt. James Estill and six of his militiamen were killed fighting a Wyandot raiding party at Little Mountain Creek near Mount Sterling.
bodyMarkdown:
On March 22, 1782, Captain James Estill and about two dozen Kentucky militiamen fought a Wyandot war party at Little Mountain Creek, near present Mount Sterling. The clash, known as the Battle of Little Mountain or Estill's Defeat, was among the bloodiest on the Kentucky frontier. Estill was killed, and the fight's outcome has been argued over ever since.

## The pursuit

An account of [the Battle of Little Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Little_Mountain) says Estill received word from [Benjamin Logan](/stories/benjamin-logan/) on March 19 that a Wyandot war party had been seen near Boonesborough. He gathered about 40 men to search for it. While they were away, the Wyandots struck nearby settlements, including Estill's Station, where they killed 14-year-old Jennie Glass and captured Monk Estill, a man enslaved by James Estill.

Monk persuaded the war party that the fort was fully manned, though only women, children and one sick man were inside. The Wyandots withdrew. Estill then took up the chase, camped at Little Mountain, and caught up with the [Wyandot](/stories/wyandot-on-kentuckys-northern-frontier/) party with 25 men.

## The battle

The two sides fought across the creek for nearly two hours. The Wyandot leader, named in one account as Sourehoowah, was reportedly shot in the first volley and urged his men on as he lay dying.

When the Wyandots began to cross, Estill split his men into three groups. Lieutenant William Miller, commanding the left, fled with his men, leaving the flank open. The Wyandots overran the remaining militia. Estill, already wounded three times, was killed in hand-to-hand fighting.

## Counting the dead

The sources disagree on the toll. Estill and six others were killed. The Kentucky Historical Society's [“Estill's Defeat” marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/estills-defeat) says Estill and 7 of his 25 men died fighting a band of 25 Wyandots.

Wyandot losses were also heavy. Monk Estill, who escaped during the battle, reportedly said 17 Wyandots were killed and two wounded.

## Aftermath

Miller became the scapegoat for the defeat and never returned to answer his accusers. Monk Estill carried a wounded militiaman, James Berry, nearly 25 miles back to the station. He was freed soon afterward by Wallace Estill and is described as the first enslaved person freed in Kentucky.

## Kentucky today

Estill County, formed in 1808, bears the captain's name; the KHS [county marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1808) calls it Kentucky's 50th county. The Estill's Defeat marker stands on US 60 at [Mount Sterling](/stories/mount-sterling-little-mountain-town/). A millstone marker traditionally marks the place of Estill's death.
